474: A few weeks ago our Bikeskills.cz team literally got its hands on SPANK handlebars with the so-called {1}VIBROCORE™ {2}core. For us it was a big unknown – we didn't know what to expect from the bars and, honestly, didn't have high expectations, because they're simply 'just' handlebars. But after the test everything changed, and now I'm thinking…. WHY NOT? I'll explain everything below.
476: The principle is simple at first glance. It's a foam of a specific density injected into the cavity of the handlebar, filling about 80% of it. Why not all of it? The ends of the bar are foam-free and ready for possible cutting, so you don't immediately cut into the Vibrocore{1}™{2}{3} {4}foam.
477: What's more interesting is that the foam has a fairly high density and is also biodegradable. The filling also increases the overall strength of the bar, which is a nice benefit, but certainly not the main goal SPANK set itself. Only when we talk about vibrations does the key word Vibrocore{1}™{2}{3} come into play.{4}
479: The first thing that comes to mind is absorbing vibrations while riding. Partly yes and partly no. The purpose of the Vibroco{1}re{2}{3}™{4} filling is not primarily to absorb vibrations (that's more what suspension forks, shocks etc. on your bike are for), but rather to change the vibration frequency. Absorbing vibrations is a small part of it, but not the main purpose of foam-filled handlebars.
480: Vibrocore™{1} {2}was developed over several years into a precisely defined type of foam that changes the frequency of vibrations transmitted from the wheels into the handlebars during riding, and from the handlebars on to the rider's hands and forearms.
481: You can find an interesting video describing the development of {1}Vibrocore{2}{3}™{4} here:
483: The frequency while riding an MTB is somewhere between 2 and 200 Hz, which is a fairly wide range. It depends on riding style and the surface you're riding on. However, most common vibrations are somewhere between 5 and 50 Hz. Every handlebar, whether carbon or aluminium, also has its own vibration frequency, so it not only nicely transmits vibrations from the wheels, frame, fork etc., but also produces its own vibration – which, simply put, creates….an amazing storm of vibrations.
484: According to the SPANK website, which describes the whole {1}Vibrocore{2}{3}™{4} system in more detail (see: https://spank-ind.com/blogs/news/vibrocore™-the-inside-story), it has been shown that vibrations with a frequency of about 8–50 Hz are dangerous for the hands, hand muscles and forearms and can cause so-called HAVS, which can gradually progress to so-called CECS. I'm not an expert or a doctor, but after a few moments on Google I saw some nasty pictures, and neither idea appeals to me at all.
485: {1}HAVS (Hand {2}{3}Arm{4}{5} {6}{7}Vibration{8}{9} Syndrome){10} is also known as {11}white finger syndrome{12}, or {13}Raynaud's{14}{15} syndrome{16}, see: {17}https://www.fyzioklinika.cz/clanky-o-zdravi/raynauduv-syndrom{18}, which often accompanies Raynaud's disease, see: {19}https://cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynaudova_nemoc{20}. White to blue fingertips, poor blood circulation and tissue damage, lack of oxygen up to tissue death. Simply nothing pleasant. This
486: syndrome often appears in professions where you work with tools that cause stronger vibrations, such as saws, drills, demolition hammers and so on. However, when riding a bike, especially an MTB on forest paths, roots and bumpy tracks, you simply can't avoid vibrations either, and everyone holds the bars firmly enough so they don't fly out of their hands.
487: {1}CECS ({2}{3}Chronic{4}{5} {6}{7}Exertional{8}{9} {10}{11}Compartment{12}{13} Syndrome){14}{15} {16}which can be a consequence of HAVS and often appears in motorsport, where a firm grip combined with vibrations from the machine is needed. However, it also appears in bodybuilders and, simply, people who pump iron. Loss of strength in the hands and forearm pain are essentially the result, quite often followed by surgery. Look up photos of CECS – it won't be a pretty sight.
489: So the foam inside the handlebar doesn't primarily absorb impacts or vibrations. That's simply not what it's there for – it changes the vibration frequency of the bar and wheel away from the dangerous frequencies mentioned, which can (though of course for some people never will) cause damage to the muscles and nerves of the hands or loss of control of the bike and so on.
490: WHAT WE TOOK AWAY FROM THE TEST
491: SPANK handlebars are among the best on the market even without {1}Vibrocore{2}{3}™{4}{5} {6}foam, which has now reached its 6th generation. The SPANK SPIKE 35 handlebar we tested fits perfectly in the hand, and its oversize 35 mm diameter suggests increased overall stiffness for Enduro or DH.
492: Now let me go back to the opening thought. When someone has devoted so much attention to something like vibrations, vibration frequency and preventing conditions like HAVS and CECS, why not take the chance to give your hands a 'longer lifespan' without pain and problems? You can believe in {1}Vibrocore™ {2}or not, but even if the bars and their internal foam helped prevent problems by just 10% – problems that may not show up on the first ride but, for example, after a long time or in old age…..then…..WHY NOT?{3}

495: Exhibitions in Travčice and the Pelhřimov records
496: This weekend was again a bit nomadic. Vlasta loaded up young guns Matouš Balík and Tobík Dolák and set off, somewhat unexpectedly, towards Pelhřimov, where another edition of the Pelhřimov Records was taking place. Although our team has many registered records, we had never been to this event. Moreover, the invitation came only a few days in advance. On the packed square it looked like rain at first, but in the end we rode the whole show in sunshine right on the main stage, and we even managed to use our trailer for jumping over and dropping off. People enjoyed the show and hopefully we'll be invited to future editions.
497: But the Pelhřimov exhibition might not have happened at all – it was only thanks to Martin Šimůnek's freed-up schedule that the Travčice exhibition worked out too. Martin and unicyclist Dominik also had a packed crowd, even though it was just a small village sports event. They also definitely sent more photos than Vlasta's part of the team, but hopefully something else will arrive.
498: Before the exhibition Vlasta went to check out the new Rock Machine bikes, which got new colours, and a luxurious new Enduro and E-bike were on display too. Thanks to LSK for the invitation.
500: We have our first camp dedicated to women and girls who wanted to improve their technique and style on the bike behind us. Almost ideal sunny weather – meaning neither cold nor hot – underlined the relaxed atmosphere and gave everyone the energy to progress on the pump track, in the skills centre and on a ride in the surrounding forests.
501: Katarína and Vlasta were available, as well as Mára and Lukáš. The latter dived into the action literally headfirst, and besides an exhibition after lunch he also demonstrated the master carpenter's mistake – a silly crash. He came away with a bruised finger.
502: Lunch was also sorted successfully, and Mára's workshop took place in relaxed mode. All day everyone had the chance to compete for MALOJA jerseys donated by LEVELSPORTKONCEPT. The condition for winning wasn't to be the best but to make the biggest progress. In the end the instructors' vote produced two winners – congratulations.
503: We look forward to the next camp for intermediate men on 23 May. We're also preparing a trail version for women and men.
504: In the meantime Vlasta and club colleagues Petr Jeřicha and Martin Vavřinec popped over to Czech Television for the programme Náš venkov to present the Kolovraty – Mnichovice cycle path.
505: A triple exhibition load – Pankrác / Doksy / Letňany
506: After several days of individual training, a Saturday on the Trial bike and 3 exhibitions awaited me and the guys. It started in the morning in Prague at the Craft Run, which happened to be supported by Gatorade. Here, for now, just with my colleague Lukáš Valný. You could tell people were a bit scared of the weather, but as it warmed up the number of visitors grew, and our show after Honza Weber already had a pretty decent crowd.
507: We quickly threw everything into the car and set off to meet Martin Šimůnek in Doksy near Česká Lípa, where the traditional meet of Škoda cars and car tuning was taking place. The organisers slowly squeezed us through the packed camp to the spot where the main participants of our show were already gathering – kids from a children's home for abused and neglected children. Hopefully Martin, Lukáš and I brought a little joy into their lives. I mustn't forget my son Marty, who rode his first exhibition here, and Nikolka and Elinka, who helped and took photos the whole time.
508: The exhibition ran long, so we had barely packed the obstacles before we were on the way to Letňany in Prague, where the Pivobraní beer festival was on. In a really packed atmosphere we launched an exhibition for all the beer lovers and fans of the various goodies on offer at the stalls. This time we rode the exhibition at a slightly more action-packed pace.
